title: blits vocabulary
subject: blits, the effects-schema package: the roles of its schema, the verbs of its API, and the operations of its channels

gloss.lead: What one call to a piece returns: a record with one slot per channel of the table.
items: The piece fills only the slots it drives and leaves the others empty. Flicker fills gain; slam fills position and \scale; hue fills color.
Which slots come back is the piece’s own decision, and it may differ from call to call.
A filled slot is a change from the channel’s rest: gain: 0.1 means multiply by 0.1, not set to 0.1.
An empty slot means no contribution. The merge skips it.

gloss.lead: One slot in an offset: one name, one rule for combining two values written into it.
items: Gain is a channel whose values multiply. Position is a channel whose triples \add.
The rule belongs to the channel, so what happens when two pieces write the same slot is settled once, not per piece.
One name and one rule whatever the shape of the values: gain is a single number, position is three under one rule.

gloss.lead: The full list of channels one kind of item can be moved on, each with its rule.
items: klieg has three: a pose table for a letter, a part table for a tube run or a flake, a lighting table for the whole frame.
A piece writes into one table. A mix runs over one table.
It is a closed list: a piece cannot write a channel the table does not have.
In hero games a character's kit is its fixed set of abilities, the same for everyone who plays it; a rig is that for one kind of subject.

gloss.lead: The thing being driven.
items: A letter, a tube run, a wheel wedge, a page.
A piece is asked about one item at a time, and a sample is the answer for one item.
A system that drives a single thing, such as klieg’s lighting, has one item.

gloss.lead: A reusable rule for how one item moves away from rest over time. A track is one of them playing.
items: Given where it is in its period and what the item looks like now, it returns an offset: values on the channels it drives, and nothing on the others.
It declares which channels it writes, so what it may touch is known before it runs.
It may keep state per item — a strike burning down, a warm-up, a hash walk — advanced by the gap since that item last caught up.
It knows nothing about the others. Everything it emits is relative to rest, and that is what lets several of them run at once without coordinating.

gloss.lead: One piece, playing.
items: It has its own start time, rate and loop setting, its own weight over time, and its own set of items.
Two tracks of the same piece are two clocks and two weights.
A track is what a host adds to a mix and later stops.
What a host passes to add is a track spec; the track is the live thing, holding the clock, the weight and the piece's state per item.

gloss.lead: The plain object of parameters handed to a call.
items: A track spec is what add takes — piece, items, rate, weight, fade. The track is what the mix builds from it, and what the handle points at.
Fixed, and used the same way everywhere: whatever a call takes as a bag of named parameters is that thing's spec.

gloss.lead: Everything a host holds: the tracks that are playing, over one table.
items: Once a frame the host tells it what time it is. Nothing advances at that call: each item catches up by the whole gap the first time it is sampled afterward.
Then, for each item it wants to draw, the host samples@v it and gets back one resolved record.

gloss.lead: A function of one item, read once a frame, that yields a number from 0 to 1 from something outside the clock.
items: Where the number comes from: how close the cursor is, how long it has hovered, a level the host writes, another track’s state.
They compose, and some of them hold state: peak takes the largest of several, slew follows its input no faster than a rate limit, gate holds its value inside a band.
It plugs in at two places and nowhere else — as a track’s weight, so an effect follows the cursor, and as the selector blend@v shares weight out by.

A piece is also a function of one item read once a frame. The difference is what comes back: a piece writes an offset across channels, a signal yields one scalar, and where that scalar is allowed to land is fixed.

gloss.lead: Whatever decided a track should exist: the app side of the call, named but not defined.
items: A score, a handler on an event, a sequence handing over, another system entirely. The package owns none of them and requires nothing of them.
It is here so the vocabulary can say where a track came from. There is no source type, no interface and nothing to implement: a source calls add@v and gets back a handle.

gloss.lead: The source a host keeps that holds the whole plan: what plays, over what, and when.
items: It supplies the two things the package otherwise takes as given — the timing, and the cast of items that will be driven.
What it looks like is not knowable here. klieg’s is spread across handlers and a Timeline; another app’s may be a document, a route table, a state machine.
Being ahead of time is what distinguishes it: a handler knows only now, a score knows the shape of the whole run.
It comes inside blits (decided 2026-09-29), provided it depends on no implementation: one per source, placing voices by pins, knowing when each plays and never what it contributes.

roles.title: Pin
roles.description: what fixes a voice in time

gloss.lead: What fixes one edge of a voice to a time, or to an edge another voice has.
items: At most one on each side: start or in, and out or end.
It takes a query, so it is rerun while bound; once its target leaves it keeps the time it last resolved to.
pin: { in: 12_400 } is fully in by 12.4 s.

roles.title: Event
roles.description: a named instant a source raises

gloss.lead: A named instant a source raises, which a pin can target: blits times it and never reads what it means.
items: Scheduled in a score, it is known ahead: a read ahead sees it and a voice can be fully in by it.
Fired by the host when something happens, such as a click or a reply, it is unknown until it fires: a voice pinned to it waits, and anything depending on it reads as held.
What fires one on a condition is a trigger. A trigger on a channel's value is the host's: it watches the condition and fires the event.

roles.title: Edge
roles.description: an instant on a voice's span

gloss.lead: One of the four instants a voice has on the mix clock: start (fade-in begins), in (full weight), out (fade-out begins) and end (gone).
items: What a pin fixes, and what a query answers with.
start and in are always known ahead; out and end once the voice has a finite length or a scheduled fade.
In blocking an actor hits a mark; a pin lands a voice on one the same way.

roles.title: Label
roles.description: a voice's name in its score

gloss.lead: The name a source gives a voice, so another voice can be placed against it without holding its handle.
items: A string blits never reads.
Namespaced by score: a bare label names a voice in the same score, { score, key } one in another.
Called key in the sketch, which collides with the keys patch form.

roles.title: Tag
roles.description: a label a source attaches for queries

gloss.lead: A word a source attaches to its voices so a query from anywhere can select them as a set.
items: Many voices share a tag; a voice has many tags.
What lets one source place against another's material without knowing its labels.
A tag can be declared to fold its voices as alternatives, which is what a group is today.

roles.title: Query
roles.description: what a pin asks the score

gloss.lead: A question the merged score answers with a time: a selector, an edge, and, where more than one voice matches, a reducer.
items: It reads only what the score knows: labels, scores, the channels a voice writes, tags. Never a channel's value.
The same queries say what plays at a time and where the next event is.

gloss.lead: What narrows a query's matches to the one voice whose edge a pin follows. The selector says which voices qualify; the reducer says which of them counts.
items: It compares only times on the mix clock: earliest and latest by the edge the query names, next and previous as the earliest after now and the latest before it.
It never reads what a voice contributes, so it cannot pick the loudest or the one with the most gain.
No match answers nothing, and the pinned voice stays pending until something matches.

gloss.lead: What a look@v returns: the mix at a reading other than the one the host last stepped@v to, ahead or back, which never touches the live mix.
items: Each subject's state is copied the first time it is asked about, then carried forward one stretch at a time.
It answers the way the live mix does: sample@v a subject for its pose, and sure@v it for how far each channel can be trusted.

roles.title: Certainty
roles.description: how far a view can be trusted

gloss.lead: How far a view's answer can be trusted, told channel by channel, since one channel can be certain while the next is a guess.
items: exact: nothing uncertain went into it. The mix will show this.
stepped: something the clock drives, such as a slew chasing a sine, moved between the events the view jumped across. Close, and off by at most what a finer step would fix.
held: something from outside the clock went into it, such as the pointer or a level the host sets. Nobody knows its future, so the view assumed it stays where it is now.
A channel takes the least certain of the voices that wrote it.

roles.title: Checkpoint
roles.description: a kept state to read back from

gloss.lead: A copy of a subject's state kept at a time, so a read back can step forward from it rather than from the voice's start.
items: How many are kept is a cost to tune, not a design question.
Without one, a read back starts where the voice's state was made.

gloss.lead: The time between two events the score knows: a voice starting, a fade ending, a loop running out.
items: A read steps once per stretch, however long.
Exact across it when what the state follows holds still; stepped when a clock-driven input moves inside it.

gloss.lead: The remote for one track: what add@v gives back, so you can point at that one later.
items: Through it you set the track’s weight and rate, seek@v its clock, and stop@v it. Each lands on the next frame, never mid-frame.
Its done promise resolves once the track has left the mix by any route, so a host can await an effect finishing.

gloss.lead: The code behind a mix that does the stepping and the sampling.
items: The mix is the interface. An engine is one implementation of it.
One ships, running pieces on the CPU.
A later one could bake keyframes to CSS or fill a GPU buffer, and a host would not know the difference.

gloss.lead: One complete area of driven behavior: a table, the item type it drives, and the mix that runs them.
items: klieg's motion, effects and lighting are three systems in one host; wod's transitions are one.
A system is what a consumer declares and could do without: dropping one takes its table, its items and its mix with it, and leaves the others standing.
Two systems never share a mix, so a track belongs to exactly one.

gloss.lead: Whatever meets the package’s three obligations: it owns the frame loop, it draws, and it keeps the items alive.
items: Once a frame it steps@v the mix, then samples@v every item it means to draw and writes what comes back onto a mesh, a wedge or a gain node. The package draws nothing itself.
Items must keep their identity between frames. State is held against the object, so an item rebuilt every frame silently starts over.

That is the whole contract. Deciding what plays is a source’s job, not this one, and everything else klieg does — laying out letters, holding a timeline, choosing when to strike — is the app, not the host.
klieg, wod, sherpa and magicsmoke each contain one. None of them is one.

gloss.lead: A channel’s value for nothing happening.
items: For a channel that multiplies it is 1. For one that adds it is 0. Color has none.
A track at weight 0 pulls its values to rest.
An item no track reaches samples@v to rest on every channel.

gloss.lead: How much of a track is on, from 0 to 1.
items: Its offset is pulled toward rest by the weight before the merge: at 0 the track contributes nothing, at 1 all of it.
A ramp in time is a fade. A signal is an effect that follows the cursor.
It is the only knob the mix turns.

gloss.lead: What one item looks like at one frame, after every track has been merged.
items: A frame is a moment: one tick of the clock across the whole mix. A sample is one cell of it: one item at that tick. A frame with 24 tube runs holds 24 samples.
Every channel of the table is filled. Where an offset is partial, a sample is complete.
The host reads it and writes it to the screen: a mesh’s position, a wedge’s opacity, a gain node’s level.
klieg’s name for it, ResolvedOffset, says how it is made rather than what it is.

gloss.lead: What one track actually does to one item in one frame, once its weight is applied.
items: The track’s offset after its weight has been applied. Not a fraction of the whole: two tracks each contributing gain 0.1 leave the item at 0.01.
The merge combines contributions channel by channel, starting from rest.

gloss.lead: The relevant state of the world in this frame, as a piece sees it, for one item.
items: Everything a piece may read but did not compute, and nothing else. It is handed in beside the phase and the item.
Shared by the whole frame: the clock, and the time since the last frame.
Particular to the track: how long it has been playing, which pass this is, its weight.
Particular to this item: the piece’s own state for it.
Whatever the host adds, such as where the cursor is.

roles.title: Reading
roles.description: the mix clock's value at a frame

gloss.lead: The value of the mix clock the host reports: what sync is handed each frame and what a look ahead or back is taken at.
items: A reading is reported, never set, and only goes forward; nothing in the mix moves the clock.
A voice's elapsed is the other clock, and it is a position: seek sets it. Mix time is not.
Milliseconds on any monotonic clock the host likes.

gloss.lead: How long one pass of a piece lasts, in milliseconds.
items: The phase runs from 0 to 1 across it and then wraps.
A period of 0 means the piece does not repeat: the phase stays at 0 and the piece reads elapsed time instead.

gloss.lead: Where a track is within its period, from 0 to 1, wrapping.
items: The first thing a piece is handed, and what stagger shifts per item.
klieg’s cycle already calls its per-letter offset phase.
Fixed, not up for a vote. The cost is renaming klieg’s onPhase and PhaseEvent, the enter–active–exit events sherpa consumes, which Mike has said klieg will pay.

gloss.lead: A label shared by tracks that are alternatives in time.
items: klieg’s enter, active and exit are one group.
Within a group the weights are capped to sum to at most 1, so a crossfade is always a \blend of the two and never a pile-up.
Tracks meant to stack stay out of groups.
Tracks that must run in order belong to a sequence, not a group.
Proposed to fold into tag: a tag declared to blend its voices as alternatives, rather than a second kind of label. A voice blends in at most one.

Read as a locus: the members are the answers to one question about what the subject is doing (how it moves, what mood it is in), and every blend of them lies in the space they span, the way alleles share one locus. That space grows and shrinks as answers are cued and leave. The question is an axis of behavior, not a channel; a group spans every channel its members write.

gloss.lead: An ordered chain of tracks that hand over, one to the next.
items: klieg's enter, active and exit, in that order: each track's exit is the next one's cue.
A group only caps what is on at once. A sequence also says what comes next, and when the whole thing is done.
It finishes, which a group never does — a handle for the sequence resolves once the last track has left.
Now one arrangement a score can hold, rather than an object of its own.

gloss.lead: Put a track into the mix, built from a spec.
items: It begins on the next frame unless its start time says otherwise.
Returns the handle.

gloss.lead: Take a track out of the mix.
items: Its weight ramps to 0 over the track’s fade first — a number of milliseconds, set when the track was added or passed here.
Or, if asked, it waits per item until the track is at rest and leaves without a fade.

gloss.lead: The host tells the mix what time it is: one \clock reading, once a \frame.
items: It takes an absolute reading on a monotonic \clock, never an amount elapsed. klieg passes its own Clock.now(), wod passes performance.now(), a test passes integers.
Nothing advances at the call. It publishes the reading, and each item catches up the first time it is sampled@v afterward, by the gap since that item last caught up.
The gap is never subdivided. An item left unasked for three \frames catches up once, by the whole gap, not three times: nothing is lost and nothing is replayed.
The same reading twice changes nothing, and every sample between readings answers from the one \frame.

The reading only ever goes forward. A piece’s state is an accumulation with no inverse, so no reading un-burns a strike or un-slews a value. Moving a track within its period is seek@v’s job, and that moves phase, not this.

gloss.lead: Ask for one item’s resolved record at the current frame.

verbs.title: look
verbs.description: read the mix at another time

gloss.lead: Open a view of the mix at a reading other than the synced one.
items: Ahead or back; the live mix is untouched.
Takes an optional finer step.

verbs.title: sure
verbs.description: how sure a view is, per channel

gloss.lead: Ask a view how far its answer for one subject can be trusted, channel by channel.
items: Returns exact, stepped or held per channel.

gloss.lead: Move one track’s own clock to a given elapsed time.
items: Nothing else in the mix moves.

gloss.lead: Put several tracks in at once whose weights are shared out by one signal.
items: As the signal runs from 0 to 1, the result moves from the first piece to the last.
The same as adding each of them, with one signal sharing the weights out.

gloss.lead: Stop every track in the mix at once.
items: Takes a fade in milliseconds: every weight ramps to 0 over it, and the tracks leave when they get there. Without one they leave on the next frame.
The same as stopping each track through its handle, with one fade for all of them.

gloss.lead: Throw away the state the mix keeps for one item.
items: For an item that will not be sampled@v again, such as a letter that has left the screen.

gloss.lead: Combine two values on one channel into one.
items: For gain, multiply. For position, \add. For dark, take the larger. For color, take the later.
The channel decides, not the pieces.

gloss.lead: Pull a value toward its channel’s rest by a weight from 0 to 1.
items: At 1 the value is untouched. At 0 it is rest.
Only a channel that has a rest can do this.
lerp with one end pinned to rest: scale(v, w) is lerp(rest, v, w). That is the whole reason a channel without a rest cannot do it.

gloss.lead: Find the value a given fraction of the way from one value to another on a channel.
items: How a retargeted track moves from wherever an item is now.
The only way a channel without a rest, such as color, can change smoothly.

gloss.lead: Merge every contribution reaching one item into one resolved record.
items: Channel by channel, starting from rest.
What Σ stands for in the relations, and what an engine exists to compute.
join, taken down the list two at a time, from rest. The channel's rule does the work; fold only supplies the order and the starting value.

relations.gloss: a set of values, and how two of them combine
the axes one kind of thing can move on
one value on some of those axes; the \rest absent
what one effect says about one thing at one instant
a track's own clock, normalized to its period
an effect given a start, a speed, a volume, a set of things
how much of a track is on: a ramp in time, or an outside reading
the offset scaled toward rest, per channel
everything reaching one item this frame, folded, per channel

relations.formula: mix = { track₁ … trackₘ } over one table
relations.gloss: what a host holds and steps
a chain that hands over and finishes; a group only caps what is on at once
one complete area a host drives: what can be moved, what is moved, and what is moving it
the knobs a host may turn between frames
whatever computes the fold; one ships

algebra.body:
A channel c is a value set Vc with four operations:

joinc : Vc × Vc → Vc
restc ∈ Vc  optional
scalec : Vc × [0, 1] → Vc  present iff rest is
lerpc : Vc × Vc × [0, 1] → Vc

Laws: join is associative; join(v, rest) = v; scale(v, 1) = v; scale(v, 0) = rest; lerp(a, b, 0) = a; lerp(a, b, 1) = b. A channel with rest is a monoid. mul is (ℝ, ·, 1); sum is (ℝ, +, 0); max is (ℝ≥0, max, 0); last is (V, second-argument) with no identity.

Strictly, only join is an operation on Vc, in the algebraist’s sense of a map from the set to itself: binary, with rest as its identity. Scale is not: it takes a value and a number from a different set, which makes it an action of [0, 1] on the channel, as scalars act on a vector space, with scale(v, 1) = v as its unit law. Lerp is a family of binary operations indexed by u; on a channel that adds it is the convex combination (1 − u)a + ub and not primitive at all, and it is primitive only where there is no addition to build it from, as for color. Fold, below, is join iterated. A channel is therefore an algebra: a set carrying its operations.

A finite indexed family of channels, T = {c1, …, cn}. It defines two spaces:

ΔT = ∏c (Vc ∪ {⊥})  partial: any channel may be absent
ΣT = ∏c Vc  total: every channel present

Δ is what pieces write; Σ is what a host reads. Both are products, so every operation on a table is the channel's operation applied coordinate-wise, with ⊥ treated as "contributes nothing" (it is the unit of join on Δ).
An element i of an arbitrary set I. The package never looks inside it; identity is all it uses, for state. A system with no item dimension has I = {∗}.

One element δ ∈ ΔT: the return value of one call to one piece for one item at one instant.

δ = p(t, i, ctx)

Two offsets on the same item compose by joinc per channel. The resolved value a host reads is an element of ΣT, not ΔT; klieg's ResolvedOffset lives there, and the sheet's starred sample is a name for it.

A period dp ∈ ℝ≥0 and a function of normalized time:

p : [0, 1] × I × Ctx → ΔT

Pure in its arguments. A stateful piece carries a state set S with an initial state per item and a \step function S × ℝ → S; the mix threads si through ctx, so p stays a function of what it is given. A wrapper is a function Piece → Piece.

σ : I × Ctx → [0, 1]

The same shape as a piece with one channel on [0, 1] and no period. Combinators are pointwise: peak = max, gate = \step function, slew = a stateful σ.

A tuple k = (p, s, r, w, on): a piece, a start time, a rate, a weight function, and a target predicate I → {0, 1}. Its own clock and its contribution on an item at time τ:

elapsedk(τ) = (τ − s) · r
t = (elapsed mod dp) / dp
wk : ℝ → [0, 1]  a ramp in τ, or σ(i, ctx)
contribk(i, τ) = wk(τ) ⊙ p(t, i, ctx)   where w ⊙ δ = (scalec(δc, w))c

On a channel with no rest, ⊙ is a gate: δc if w > ε, else ⊥. Two tracks of one piece are two tuples; they share p and nothing else.

A finite set of tracks M over one table, and the fold that resolves them:

sampleM(i, τ) = ⨁c  joinc* { contribk(i, τ)c : k ∈ M, onk(i) }   ∈ ΣT

join* folds from restc, so an item nothing reaches samples@v to rest. Associativity is what makes the fold order-free; last is the one channel where order matters, and it is by declaration. A group G ⊆ M with a cap rescales its weights by 1 / max(1, Σk∈G wk) before ⊙.

The four \blends, in these terms: fade is wk a ramp in τ; alternatives are wk = hatk(σ) with Σk hatk = 1; handover removes k from M at the first τ where p(t, i, ctx) = rest; retarget replaces \stop 0 of a keyframe piece with sampleM∖{k}(i, s) and moves by lerpc.
A reference to one k ∈ M with write access to s, r and w, and the event k ∉ M. It \adds nothing to the algebra; it is how a host mutates a tuple between frames.

An implementation of sample:

E : (T, M, τ) → (I → ΣT)

Two engines are interchangeable exactly when they agree on every (T, M, τ) whose pieces both can run. That equation is the port's test: Emixer must equal klieg's three merge functions on every input klieg's suites already exercise.

why.title: Why offset
why.body:
It is klieg's own word, and it says the one thing that matters about what a piece emits: the value is relative to rest, not absolute. A piece that writes nothing contributes nothing; position \rests at 0 and gain at 1; the merge is a fold of relative contributions. That is what lets layers compose without knowing about each other.

It is wrong in two places. Color replaces rather than \offsets, and a retargeted keyframe track holds absolute \stops. It also covers two things at once: what a piece emits, a partial relative record, and what the mix returns, a resolved absolute one. klieg calls those PartOffset and ResolvedOffset. A rename can split them, and the first term below carries both.

relations.title: The roles, as relations
relations.body:
How the quantities stand to each other, one line each, before any of them is defined precisely. Read = as "is made of" or "is computed from", and Σ as "the fold of", using whatever rule the channel has.

Two of these carry the whole design. contribution = weight ⊙ offset is where every fade, crossfade and \blend-between-alternatives happens, because weight is the only thing a mix varies. sample = rest ⊕ Σ contribution is where layering happens, and the rule inside Σ belongs to the channel, so two effects on one axis combine the same way whoever wrote them.

algebraIntro.title: The roles, as algebra
algebraIntro.body:
The same relations with their sets and laws made explicit. Nothing here is beyond a product of sets and a fold; the point is that every \blend in the package is one of the four channel operations applied under the fold.

Read across, the whole package is: pieces produce elements of Δ; tracks \weight them with ⊙; a mix folds them with join into Σ; an engine is any function that computes that fold. The channel table is the only place arithmetic is defined, so a consumer that needs a new \blend \adds a channel with a new (join, rest, scale, lerp), never a new rule in the mix.

sets.title: Six consistent sets
sets.body:
Six fields each give a complete vocabulary for the whole pipeline. The learning column lands on the same three roles the geometry does, with the same split: feature for one coordinate, feature space for all of them, feature vector for one point; and it gives adjustment, ensemble and epoch. The physics column is the one that says what the mix is: forces from independent sources superposing on a body into one resultant, with a field assigning one to every point. Its cost is that forces \add and half the channels multiply, and that force is a flag and a physics-engine word in the same codebases. Any one column reads as a system; mixing columns reads as arbitrary, with one exception: the algebra column is strong exactly where the arithmetic lives (domain, axis, term, curve) and strained where the host lives, so a set that is mathematical on the left of the fold and plain on the right matches what each part is.

domain.title: On domain for the channel set
domain.body:
Revised. The objection below measured the word against the piece, whose output is the offset space. The table defines join, scale and lerp, and those act on the value space, so for them it is the domain in the strict sense, and so is the mix's fold. The klieg collision is not a constraint: Mike said on 2026-09-15 that klieg changes if it has to, provided blits produces something good, so the gradient's domain renames if this word is taken. domain now ranks with rig: the one for a mathematical register, the other for the puppet.

The original note, kept for the record. It works as English and has two collisions, one of them in klieg.

  • Math puts it at the wrong end. A clip maps time and a target to an offset. The offset space is the codomain; the domain is time. d3 uses the words the same way: domain is input, range is output. Anyone who knows either reads "the pose domain" as time.
  • klieg already uses it. The gradient's letter domain is the span a color ramp runs over. A second, unrelated domain in the same package's types is a collision a reader hits once and distrusts forever.

What it gets right is the feel: "the pose domain" says the area where pose values live, which is better than table, which says data structure. Two words keep that feel without the collisions. space is the math word for the output side: "pose space", "part space", "presence space" all read as the set of values a thing can take. rig says it from the animation side: the set of controls a thing is driven through.

recommendation.title: What I would take
recommendation.body:
recommendation

Mathematical where the arithmetic lives, plain where the host lives. domain for the channel set, axis for one channel, term for what a piece returns, curve for the piece itself; with them, origin for rest and coefficient for weight. On the host side the DAW words stay: track, mix, signal, handle, engine, and item for the driven thing until a better one turns up. The page opens on this set.

In one sentence: a curve returns a term; the coefficient scales it toward the origin; the mix folds the terms along each axis of the domain. Every word in it is doing exact work.
